applicability: Any positive integer n, of any length. Write its decimal digits from the RIGHT as d0 (units), d1 (tens), d2 (hundreds), ...; form the alternating sum A(n) = d0 - d1 + d2 - d3 + ... Then n ≡ A(n) (mod 11), so n is divisible by 11 EXACTLY WHEN A(n) is a multiple of 11 — where 0, +11, -11, +22, ... all count as multiples. Direction matters for the value of A(n) (it must start at the units digit and alternate leftwards), but not for the yes/no verdict, since running it from the left only ever flips the sign of A(n). The 'exactly when' is asserted here only over the exhaustively checked finite domain 1 ≤ n ≤ 999999; see nulls[].
carry_case: 2915. The alternating sum is 5 - 1 + 9 - 2 = 11, which is NOT 0, yet 2915 = 11 × 265 is divisible by 11. So the tempting simplified form of the rule — 'the plus/minus digits must cancel to zero' — gives a false negative. The pass condition is 'A(n) is a multiple of 11', not 'A(n) = 0'. The same break appears with a negative total: 90728 gives 8 - 2 + 7 - 0 + 9 = 22, and 209 gives 9 - 0 + 2 = 11; both are divisible by 11 while failing the 'must be zero' form.

nulls.reason: The rule is claimed as an 'exactly when' for all positive integers, but core/verify/theorems.json whitelists no theorem about alternating digit sums modulo 11 (base-b-digit-sum-congruence covers digit sums mod b-1 = 9, not mod b+1 = 11). Per §3.2 an unproven universality claim is not accepted on assertion, so the claim is stated only over the exhaustive finite domain 1 ≤ n ≤ 999999, which the generator check enumerates in full. No claim is made outside that domain.
